extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers; critics and students of the novel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on creating and evaluating the formal unity, time/space handling, and method of presentation in long fiction (the novel). Focuses on how subject, form, character, time, and method must be controlled to produce a coherent novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-made book: subject and form coincide
rubrics_metrics.description: “The well-made book is the book in which the subject and the form coincide and are indistinguishable — the book in which the matter is all used up in the form, in which the form expresses all the matter.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a novel by whether its form has used up its matter; if form and subject disagree, material is superfluous or wanting. Anti-pattern: a book whose form fails to do justice to its idea (e.g., parts that seem irrelevant to the central subject).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid wasteful, loose, unstructural form
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of wasteful form is based on the injury done to the story — the loss of its full potential value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to material that weakens the central story by being irrelevant, excessive, or underdeveloped. Example: War and Peace is criticised here as 'wasteful of its subject' because it imports another story that diminishes clarity and development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity: the novel must have one subject expressible in a phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject, one and whole and irreducible — a novel cannot begin to take shape till it has this for its support. 'What was the novelist’s intention, in a phrase?' If it cannot be put into a phrase it is no subject for a novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The subject's size or complexity may be large, but it must have a discernible unity. Until the subject is known there is nothing to be said of the form; form depends on subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single design: all material must serve the purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: All the great wealth of the material should be brought into one design; otherwise the book loses sharp relief and coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange and prune material so every scene and incident contributes to the design. Anti-pattern: material that distracts from or dilutes the main design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject must be fixed for controlled method
rubrics_metrics.description: For careful consideration of method a book is needed in which the subject is absolutely fixed and determined (Flaubert's Madame Bovary praised for this).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix the subject early so subsequent choices of phrasing and arrangement serve a stable purpose. Advantage: clearer appraisal of craft when subject does not shift during composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should be representative and feel part of a larger world
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole point of the action is in its representative character, its universality; characters should be choice examples whose attachment to the general drama of life is clearly seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render characters so they are typical without seeming utterly exceptional; their place in the world should be visible. Example: Tolstoy’s characters 'inhabit our world' and extend beyond the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate horizon/setting to the fable
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether to give a marked horizon (a self-contained world) or an open, expansive scene depends on the nature of the fable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose atmospheric scope to suit the story: an intimate closed world may be best for certain tales; a wide, continuous space suits epics of social life. Anti-pattern: mismatching vast panorama to a story that needs containment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create the sense of continuity of space and daylight when required
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuous sense of space (open sky, daylight, an unchecked communication with the rest of the world) can be essential to a book's motive and must be achieved by method, not excessive description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide freedom and latitude of movement for characters to make them feel part of an unlimited world. Note: this can be achieved without heavy descriptive passages — through the author's handling of characters and scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give characters freedom/latitude rather than excessive literal description
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of a large world comes not from mere multiplication of names or descriptive detail but from giving characters an obvious latitude of movement in an open world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid piling on description; instead allow characters to act and imply the larger world by their relations and freedoms. Anti-pattern: heavy description that nonetheless produces a cramped or overly solid small world (Balzac contrasted with Tolstoy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent passage of time through the book's structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The passage of time, its effect, must be represented in the build of the whole book; the form of time is to be represented, not merely the contents in order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't rely on mere aggregation of events or announcements ('years have fled'); ensure the lines and masses of the book show time's movement. If time is essential, the novel's shape must make that apparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray both continuous lapse and cyclical sweep of time
rubrics_metrics.description: Time's double effect — its uninterrupted lapse and the cycle (rise and fall) of which the chosen stretch is a segment —must be made perceptible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to both steady progression (changes visible in faces, gestures, thought) and the broader curve of generations or cycles; failing to represent either weakens the central subject. Critique: Tolstoy achieves steady lapse well but treats the cyclical sweep less successfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict ageing and continuity of identity convincingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should grow older with the 'noiseless regularity of life'; their mutability must never hide their sameness — consistency should endure through change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show gradual, believable development in character across years so readers perceive passage of time in personal terms (example: Anna Karenina and Tolstoy's handling of age).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design must announce the moral/meaning — not leave it as an unconnected picture
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral or meaning of the book must reside in its design; without design scattered scenes will make no picture and the 'moral' cannot be merely the picture itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure chapters and episodes cohere to announce a reason for their collocation. Anti-pattern: a book that offers vivid scenes but refuses to adapt its parts to produce a single, announced effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistent authorial intention and method throughout
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist should behave consistently and use facts in accordance with his purpose; vacillation in attitude or handling prevents facts from expressing the intended design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid changing treatment mid-book in a way that turns representative characters into mere romance heroines or shifts the novel's function. Example: Tolstoy's change in attitude toward Natasha weakened the book's original representative purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let incidental romance or subplot undermine the central theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Bringing into the middle of the interest a particular romantic question (who will marry whom) can throw away the character's representative value and change the nature of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a character is meant to serve a larger symbolic or representative role, avoid over-emphasizing a private, particular plot that reassigns her function. Use subplots only insofar as they support the central design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the subject quiescent during composition (avoid discovering new, disruptive aspects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flaubert's method: although he might hate or resent his subject, the subject remained stable and did not present new, unforeseen demands while he wrote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to master the subject before (or early in) composition so that method and phrasing can be devoted to presentation; beware of a subject that grows unruly and forces changes of design mid-course.

rubrics_metrics.name: The art is in showing — present facts so they 'tell themselves'
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist's task is to present the story in a way that will give the effect desired; the book is not a row of facts but a single image — facts are nothing until they have been used to create that image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor 'showing' (presentation that allows the reader to infer meaning) over mere narrative statement or external attestation. Anti-pattern: narrative that depends on outside authorities or simple assertion of historic truth (like Defoe's attesting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Work phrase-by-phrase and control the manner of telling
rubrics_metrics.description: Flaubert's approach emphasizes painstaking control of phrase and manner to produce the exact effect; the critic can trace how telling is arranged when subject is fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully craft sentences and arrange incidents so the desired image and effect emerge; the craft is in selection and precise presentation rather than accumulation of facts.
